description: SHA-512 outer-length falls to default=SHA-384 constant

findings.title: Incorrect message length for SHA2-512 in HMAC outer hash calculation
findings.description: In fragment hmac_core__always_comb__assign_sha_message_length__001 (lines 207-232), the else branch handling the final hash with padded outer key computes sha_msg_len as BlockSizeSHA512in64 + 64'd384 for all cases not explicitly SHA2_256 or SHA2_384. When digest_size_i is SHA2_512, the resulting sha_msg_len is incorrect because the added constant should be 64'd512 (to account for the 512-bit inner hash output), not 64'd384. This miscalculation leads to an invalid message length value fed to the SHA engine, corrupting the outer hash for HMAC-SHA-512.
findings.security_impact: HMAC-SHA-512 produces a wrong authentication tag, potentially allowing attackers to forge messages or bypass integrity checks if the HMAC is used for security purposes.

description: wipe/cfg_block protocol: cfg_block clears on stop before done

findings.title: Race condition allowing key and configuration updates during hash start
findings.description: In the HMAC module, the `cfg_block` register indicates when a hash operation is in progress (set on `hash_start_or_continue`, cleared on `reg_hash_done` or `reg_hash_stop`). The combinational update to `secret_key_d` (fragment `hmac__always_comb__update_secret_key__001`, lines 214-227) and the sequential update to `cfg_reg` (fragment `hmac__always_ff__line_375__001`, lines 375-411) rely on `!cfg_block` to permit changes only when the engine is idle. However, `cfg_block` is a registered signal that transitions on the active clock edge. In the same clock cycle that `hash_start_or_continue` is asserted, `cfg_block` is still 0, so both `secret_key_d` and `cfg_reg` can be modified. This allows an attacker to: (a) modify a secret key word while a hash operation is starting, resulting in a key partially updated with the new value, or (b) change the configuration (`sha_en`, `endian_swap`, etc.) such that the subsequent hash uses invalid settings. These violations compromise the integrity of the HMAC computation and may lead to key leakage, unexpected output, or denial of service.
findings.security_impact: Sensitive key material may be corrupted or exposed, leading to authentication bypass or data integrity failure. Configuration tampering can cause the HMAC engine to produce incorrect results or operate with reduced security guarantees.

description: Stale completion: 127-cycle cool_down delay before hash_done_event

findings.title: Unintended latch inferred on cool_down_ct_d
findings.description: In the always_comb process (hmac.sv lines 149-195), signal cool_down_ct_d is not assigned in all branches. Specifically, it is only assigned in state DoneAwaitCmd (to 0) and in state DoneAwaitHashComplete when (!hash_running) is true. In states DoneAwaitHashDone, DoneAwaitMessageComplete, and when hash_running is true in DoneAwaitHashComplete, no assignment is made to cool_down_ct_d. This causes synthesis to infer a latch on cool_down_ct_d before its register, leading to potential simulation/synthesis mismatches, hold-time violations, and incorrect cool-down counter behavior.
findings.security_impact: Unintended latches can cause unpredictable operation of the cool-down timer, potentially affecting the timing of hash_done_event signaling and subsequent interrupt generation. This could lead to subtle protocol violations or race conditions in the HMAC security flow.

findings.title: wipe_secret write enabled on bus error instead of only on error-free transactions
findings.description: In fragment hmac_reg_top__continuous_region__declarations_or_instances__016, the write-enable for the wipe_secret register is conditionally generated as: assign wipe_secret_we = (addr_hit[8] && reg_we && reg_error);  All other register write-enables in the same design use !reg_error (e.g., key_0_we = addr_hit[9] && reg_we && !reg_error). The use of reg_error (instead of !reg_error) allows a write to proceed exactly when a bus error (address miss, write error, or integrity error) occurs. This can cause unintended wiping or corruption of security-critical secrets.
findings.security_impact: An attacker who can trigger a bus error (e.g., by accessing an invalid address or forcing an integrity failure) can write arbitrary data to the wipe_secret register, potentially erasing or overwriting cryptographic key material without authorization, leading to denial of service or bypass of security protections.

description: Missing invalid_config_atstart in err_code priority case

findings.title: Duplicate case label in error priority encoder
findings.description: In fragment 2 (hmac__always_comb__line_846__001, lines 846-876), the priority case statement contains two identical case items `hash_start_sha_disabled:` both setting `err_code = SwHashStartWhenShaDisabled`. SystemVerilog requires unique case items; duplicate labels are illegal and will cause synthesis/simulation failures or, if the tool tolerates it, the second item becomes dead code, potentially masking a required error condition.
findings.security_impact: If not caught during design verification, this bug could lead to undetected error conditions or system misbehavior, reducing the hardware’s ability to enforce secure operation.

findings.title: Combinational loop in state_mux default assignment
findings.description: In aes_cipher_core__always_comb__state_mux__001 (lines 247-255), the default branch of the unique case statement contains: state_d = (key_len_i == AES_256) ? prd_clearing_state_i : state_d; This creates a combinational loop (or infers a latch) when key_len_i != AES_256, because state_d is assigned to itself. The self-assignment causes a feedback path that can lead to synthesis warnings, X propagation in simulation, and non-deterministic hardware behavior.
findings.security_impact: If state_sel takes an undefined value (e.g., via a fault injection), the latch could hold the previous state_d value instead of transitioning to a safe state. This could leak internal state between rounds, violate clearing requirements, or be exploited to extract key material.

description: Key-clear muxes route to key_expand_out instead of prd_clearing_key_i

findings.title: KEY_DEC_CLEAR mux selects expanded key instead of clearing key
findings.description: In fragment 2 (aes_cipher_core.sv lines 459-465), the key_dec_mux always_comb block handles the KEY_DEC_CLEAR case by assigning key_dec_d = key_expand_out, while the default case assigns the intended clearing key prd_clearing_key_i. This causes the decryption key register to be loaded with expanded key material during a clear operation, violating the secure key clearing protocol. Lines 462-463 contain the bug.
findings.security_impact: Sensitive key material is not properly cleared, potentially leaving residual key data in registers accessible to attackers.

findings.title: KEY_FULL_CLEAR mux selects expanded key instead of clearing key
findings.description: In fragment 3 (aes_cipher_core.sv lines 438-446), the key_full_mux always_comb block handles the KEY_FULL_CLEAR case by assigning key_full_d = key_expand_out, while other clearing scenarios and the default case assign prd_clearing_key_i. This causes the full key register to be loaded with expanded key material during a clear operation, violating the secure key clearing protocol. Line 444 contains the bug.
findings.security_impact: Sensitive key material is not properly cleared, potentially leaving residual key data in registers accessible to attackers.

findings.title: Combinational error signal prone to glitches
findings.description: In aes_cipher_control.sv, the always_comb block 'combine_sparse_signals' computes mr_err as a purely combinational output based on comparisons of sparse signals (lines 311-339). Any skew in the arrival of mr_state_sel[i] or related signals can cause a transient mismatch, generating a glitch on mr_err. If mr_err is used directly to trigger a security alert or lock-up (as suggested by its naming and role), this glitch could lead to false alarms and denial-of-service.
findings.security_impact: An attacker could exploit timing differences or inject faults to cause a glitch on the error signal, potentially triggering a false security alert and disrupting normal operation (availability).

findings.title: Potential incorrect mix columns direction in key expansion
findings.description: In aes_cipher_core.sv, the gen_shares_round_key block instantiates aes_mix_columns with .op_i connected to CIPH_INV (lines 516-535). The name CIPH_INV strongly suggests an inverse mix columns operation. Standard AES key expansion requires forward mix columns; using the inverse direction would generate wrong round keys, breaking encryption/decryption. If CIPH_INV is a static constant, this could be a critical functional bug depending on whether the design is intended for encryption or decryption (unless a pre-inverse key expansion scheme is used).
findings.security_impact: Incorrect round keys lead to failed encryption/decryption, potentially causing data corruption or inability to recover plaintext, compromising confidentiality and integrity.

description: iv_sel rail OR-merge + iv_we un-gated during CTR
Invalid-stage key leak: exposes raw key_state_q

findings.title: Missing key_state_q update in sequential block
findings.description: In fragment keymgr_ctrl__always_ff__line_304__001 (lines 304-318), the always_ff block resets key_state_q to '0, but in the else branch it only updates key_state_ecc_q. There is no assignment of key_state_d to key_state_q. As a result, the key_state_q register never changes from its reset value (all zeros). This means all subsequent key updates, wipe operations, and state transitions are ineffective, because the combinational logic computes key_state_d from the stale zero state. The key manager will always operate on a zero key, breaking all cryptographic functions.
findings.security_impact: The key state is permanently zero, so any derived keys or operations using key_state_q are trivially weak. This completely compromises the confidentiality and integrity of key material, potentially allowing adversaries to predict or bypass security mechanisms.

findings.title: Inconsistent entropy indexing in KeyUpdateWipe
findings.description: In fragment keymgr_ctrl__always_comb__line_363__001, inside the KeyUpdateWipe case, the line 'key_state_d[i][j] = {EntropyRounds{entropy_i[j]}};' indexes the entropy_i array with the share index j. However, in the KeyUpdateRandom case, entropy_i is indexed with the CDI index i (entropy_i[i]). If entropy_i is dimensioned for the number of CDIs (as suggested by the KeyUpdateRandom usage), then using the share index j may cause out-of-bounds access or fetch the wrong entropy value. This can lead to improper wiping of key material, leaving it inadequately randomized.
findings.security_impact: Insufficient key wipe may leave recoverable key data in the state array, violating secure erasure requirements and potentially enabling key extraction after a supposed wipe operation.

description: Data-enable FSM: illegal encoding silently redirected

findings.title: Missing key_state_q register update in sequential always_ff block
findings.description: In fragment keymgr_ctrl__always_ff__line_304__001 (lines 304-318), the always_ff block updates only the ECC parity flops (key_state_ecc_q) on every clock cycle. The actual key state register key_state_q is assigned only during reset (to '0) and is never updated in the else branch. Consequently, key_state_q remains permanently at its reset value and never reflects the combinational next-state key_state_d generated by the key update logic. This renders the entire key storage and update mechanism non-functional.
findings.security_impact: The key state is stuck at zero, meaning all cryptographic operations use a known, constant zero key. An attacker can fully bypass any key-based security protections, leading to complete compromise of key management and any derived keys.

description: ECC updated without key_state_q -> stale data -> false ecc_errs

findings.title: Key state register never updated after reset
findings.description: In the always_ff block (lines 304-318), key_state_q is asynchronously reset to '0 but is never assigned a new value in the synchronous branch. The for-loop only updates key_state_ecc_q, leaving key_state_q permanently zero. Consequently, the entire key management state machine is non-functional and cannot advance beyond the reset state.
findings.security_impact: The key state is permanently zero, potentially allowing an attacker to predict or force a known key value if the design relies on key_state_q being updated securely.

findings.title: Width mismatch in entropy loading during KeyUpdateRandom
findings.description: In the KeyUpdateRandom case (lines 373-377), 'key_state_d[i][j][cnt[EntropyRndWidth-1:0]] = entropy_i[i];' assigns the entire entropy_i[i] vector (likely multi-bit as implied by replication usage elsewhere) to a 1-bit slice of key_state_d. This truncation discards all but the LSB of the entropy, corrupting the intended random key material.
findings.security_impact: The key shares are loaded with incorrect, predictable values (only a single entropy bit replicated per bit position if cnt varies, or just the LSB), severely weakening the cryptographic strength of the root key loading.

findings.title: Potential out-of-bounds array index in KeyUpdateWipe
findings.description: In the KeyUpdateWipe case (line 401), 'entropy_i[j]' is used to fill the shares, where j iterates over the number of shares. In all other entropy accesses (e.g., KeyUpdateRandom), the index is i (CDI index). If entropy_i is dimensioned only by CDIs (e.g., [0:CDIs-1]), using j may index beyond the array bounds when Shares > CDIs, leading to X propagation or incorrect data.
findings.security_impact: An out-of-bounds access could load unknown values into the key state, potentially resulting in predictable or all-X key material, undermining the wipe operation's integrity.

findings.title: TX watermark threshold shift width truncation
findings.description: In uart_core__always_comb__line_313__001 (line 321), the threshold computation 'tx_watermark_thresh = 1'b1 << uart_fifo_txilvl;' uses a 1-bit left operand. In SystemVerilog the result width is 1 bit; shifting a 1-bit value left by any amount N>0 yields 1'b0. Therefore, for any non-zero watermark level setting (uart_fifo_txilvl > 0), tx_watermark_thresh becomes 0 instead of the intended power-of-two value. Consequently, the watermark event condition 'tx_fifo_depth < tx_watermark_thresh' is never true when level > 0, leaving the TX watermark interrupt permanently deasserted.
findings.security_impact: TX watermark interrupt non-functional; can prevent firmware from refilling the UART TX FIFO in time, leading to FIFO underruns, data corruption, or denial of service if an attacker can control UART traffic patterns.

findings.title: Incorrect saturation condition for TX watermark threshold
findings.description: In uart_core__always_comb__line_313__001 (line 319), the saturation guard 'if (uart_fifo_txilvl >= (TxFifoDepthW-2))' prematurely saturates the threshold to TxFifoDepth/2. For a typical FIFO depth of 16 (TxFifoDepthW=4), this triggers at level >= 2, setting threshold=8, whereas the threshold should only saturate when the calculated 2^(uart_fifo_txilvl) exceeds 8 (i.e., at level >= 4). This causes incorrect threshold values for intermediate level settings, breaking the intended power-of-two progression.
findings.security_impact: Incorrect interrupt threshold can cause firmware to misjudge FIFO fill level, potentially leading to buffer overruns or data loss under specific traffic conditions.

description: Break FSM re-arms on single rx_in high

findings.title: Line loopback forces RX input to constant 1, breaking loopback functionality
findings.description: In fragment 2 (lines near 'assign rx_in = ...'), the multiplexer selects 1'b1 when line_loopback is active. This forces the receiver input high continuously, preventing any data reception during line loopback mode. The correct behavior should typically route the external RX pin (or looped-back TX) to the receiver, not force an idle state. This makes the line loopback test mode non-functional and can hide faults in the receiver path.
findings.security_impact: Line loopback is often used for hardware integrity tests; this bug disables those tests, potentially allowing faulty receive hardware to go undetected, leading to silent data corruption or communication failures in security-critical applications.
